en: Front engine four-wheel drive (4WD) is a safe choice compared to the other four-wheel drive drivetrain layouts, due to the increase of understeer from having the weight of the engine at the front of the car. This makes the car easier to control, as oversteer is slightly reduced.

Front engine front-wheel drive (FWD) is the most stable of the two-wheel drive drivetrain variants. The weight of the engine helps keep the front wheels on the ground, being a perfect match with front-wheel drive. This will mean oversteer is dramatically decreased, however, the car will be more prone to understeer.

Front engine rear-wheel drive (RWD) is one of the more stable rear-wheel drive drivetrain layouts, this is due to the engine being at the front of the car, that weight helps heavily reduce oversteer and therefore creates a nice, stable, balance of understeer and oversteer.

Mid engine four-wheel drive (4WD) is a great choice for drivers that can quickly get into a rhythm with their car. Having the engine in the middle of the car means the weight is distributed more evenly to each of the wheels, making the car feel balanced and creates a nice mix of understeer and oversteer.

Mid engine rear-wheel drive (RWD) is for drivers that prefer the oversteer characteristics of a RWD drivetrain, but also want some more weight towards the front of the car to assist with easier and more stable weight transfers when driving on any surface type.

Rear engine four-wheel drive (4WD) is the most agile of the other four-wheel drive drivetrain layouts. This is due to the increase in oversteer that is caused by having the weight of the engine at the rear of the car, making this 4WD drivetrain variant the one that requires the best car control from the driver.

Rear engine rear-wheel drive (RWD) is for drivers with exceptional car control, having the weight of the engine at the rear of the car substantially increases oversteer and makes understeer almost non-existent. However, this makes the car extremely agile, perfect for stages with lots of sharp corners.

Negative camber improves cornering grip but reduces straight-line traction. Removing camber will reduce cornering grip but increase straight-line traction. Positive camber may reduce steering effort but overall grip may be reduced.

Fast bump controls how the damper handles impacts from jumps & bumps. Softer allows greater absorption but the vehicle may hit the bump stop reducing stability. Firmer may prevent this but bump absorption is reduced.
Firmer will resist damper extension for more stability but the wheel may take longer to make contact with the ground. Softer will result in less resistance on extension but stability may be reduced.
Firm springs will improve body stability but bump absorption is reduced. Soft springs will reduce body stability but bump absorption is improved.

Toe in on the front increases stability at the cost of responsiveness, however too much can cause the vehicle to understeer. Toe out on the front increases turn in, however this can cause vague steering.
